gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much battery the inverter uses just by being switched on. The Renogy 2000W UPS inverter that ChatGPT showed first is rated under 18 W of self-consumption, which works out to up to 432 Wh (36 Ah at 12 V) a day before any appliance runs. That is 60% of Victron's own 720 Wh/day RV example and needs about 86 W of panel just to cover it.
standout_why: Victron's cited sizing article (victronenergy.com/knowledge-articles/2026/5/4/how-to-size-rv-solar-system) only adds 10-15% loss for 230V appliances. It gives no idle or no-load draw, no DC amps at full load, and no inverter model. The cited Renogy RV inverter installation guide gave only site navigation when fetched, with no idle or amp figures. rvtime.com could not be opened because of a certificate error, so it was not compared. None of them turns an inverter's idle draw into Wh per day, Ah per day or panel watts.
decides: This confirms ChatGPT's suggested 1,000-3,000 W range but changes how to pick within it. An RV inverter that stays on all day costs about 18 W × 24 h of battery even with nothing plugged in. So a shopper with modest solar should shut it off when idle, buy a model with a power-saving or sleep mode, or size down: Renogy's 1000W UPS model is rated under 12 W, or 288 Wh/day. Buying 3,000 W 'to be safe' for a big battery bank adds idle draw on top of the roughly 181 A DC draw at full load from a 2,000 W unit. Price per continuous watt runs from $0.14/W for the Renogy 2000W standard to $0.33/W for the REGO 3000W inverter charger.
